title: If things had been different
cando: talk about past decisions, regrets and what might have happened

about.text: Everyone has made a decision they still think about: a job they took or turned down, a move, a risk. In this lesson you look back on decisions like these, say what might have happened if you had chosen differently, and talk about regrets without sounding stuck in the past. You also read a column about a big life decision and write a reflective paragraph of your own.
goals: Say what would have happened if a past decision had been different: If I'd known, I would have waited.
Connect a past choice to your life now: If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be here today.
Talk about regrets with wish and if only, and say when something you did turned out to be unnecessary.
Read a column about a life decision and write a reflective paragraph.
Talk through a real decision: what you did, what else you might have done, and what you learned.

chapters.title: Looking back on a decision
chapters.text:
This lesson is about decisions, and about looking back on them.
First, you listen to Priya and her colleague Tomasz. Two years ago, Priya had a dilemma. She could stay in a safe job, or move to a new city for a job she really wanted.
Listen to how she talks about it now. She says: If I'd known how lonely the first winter would be, I might have waited a year. She says: I wish I'd asked more questions. And she says: I needn't have sold my car.
Notice that she is not complaining. She is thinking out loud. That is a very natural thing to do in English, with friends and at work.

chapters.title: Grammar for things that did not happen
chapters.text:
Next, the grammar. There are two parts.
Part one is the third conditional. It is about the past, and about something that did not happen. If I had known, I would have waited. I did not know, so I did not wait.
A mixed conditional joins a past choice to the present. If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be here now.
Part two is regret. Say: I wish I had asked. Or, stronger: If only I had asked. Never say: I wish I would have asked.
Last, a small pair. I needn't have worried means I worried, and it was not necessary. I didn't need to worry means it was not necessary, and usually I didn't.

chapters.title: A column about a big decision
chapters.text:
Then you read a column from a magazine. A columnist writes about their own life, in their own voice.
This writer left a stable job to start again in another city. She tells you what she gave up, what went wrong, and what she learned.
Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again for the details.
After that, you write a reflective paragraph about a decision of your own. Say what you decided, what you gave up, and how you see it now. Use one conditional and one wish.

chapters.title: Talking through a real decision
chapters.text:
In the live class, you talk through a real decision. It can be big or small: a job, a move, a course, a car, even a haircut.
Say what you did and why. Say what might have happened if you had chosen differently. Then say what you learned.
Your teacher and the other learners will ask you questions, so be ready to explain your reasons.
Try to sound calm and thoughtful. Looking back is not about blame. It is about understanding.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text about a turning point in someone's life.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.
Watch for the sentences that look back: if only, I wish, if she had known. Writers often use them at the moments that matter most.
Ask yourself: at which moment could things have gone differently? What would you have done?

warmup.prompt: You have to make a big decision: a new job, or a move. What do you trust most?
choices: a list of pros and cons
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Most people use all three. Many say they made a list, and then followed their instinct anyway.

conversation.title: Would you do it again?
conversation.setting: Tomasz has been offered a job in another city. Over coffee at work, he asks his colleague Priya about her own move two years ago.
lines: Tomasz
Can I ask you something? I've been offered a post in Glasgow, and I honestly can't decide.
Priya
Ah, the big dilemma. I know it well. Two years ago I was exactly where you are.
Tomasz
Did you weigh up the pros and cons, or did you just go with your gut feeling?
Priya
Both, really. I made lists for weeks, but in the end my instinct said go. So I took the plunge.
Tomasz
And do you ever have second thoughts?
Priya
Sometimes. If I'd known how lonely the first winter would be, I might have waited a year.
Tomasz
Really? You always seem so settled here.
Priya
I am now. But I wish I'd asked more questions about the team before I committed to the move. And I needn't have sold my car. I bought another one within three months!
Tomasz
With hindsight, would you do it again?
Priya
Yes. If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be doing work I love. I'd probably still be in a stable job that bored me, settling for less.
Tomasz
That's what worries me. My job is safe, but it isn't going anywhere.
Priya
Then don't decide on impulse, but don't be too cautious either. Every move is a bit of a gamble.
Tomasz
True. I don't believe in fate, but maybe this offer is a sign.
Priya
Maybe. Talk to the team in Glasgow first. I wish somebody had told me that.

questions.q: Why did Priya finally decide to move?
questions.a: Her instinct told her to go.
wrong: Her manager asked her to go.
She needed money from selling her car.
questions.why: She says: in the end my instinct said go.

questions.q: What does Priya say about selling her car?
questions.a: It wasn't necessary: she soon bought another one.
wrong: She sold it to pay for the move.
questions.why: I needn't have sold my car: she sold it, and it turned out to be unnecessary.

questions.q: What does Priya advise Tomasz to do?
questions.a: Talk to the team in Glasgow before he decides.
questions.why: She says: Talk to the team in Glasgow first.

phrases.text: Did you weigh up the pros and cons?
phrases.use: Asking how carefully somebody made a decision.

phrases.text: If I'd known, I might have waited a year.
phrases.use: Saying what you would have done with better information.

phrases.text: I wish I'd asked more questions.
phrases.use: Saying you regret something you did not do.

phrases.text: I needn't have sold my car.
phrases.use: Saying you did something that turned out to be unnecessary.

phrases.text: With hindsight, would you do it again?
phrases.use: Asking somebody to judge a past decision now.

phrases.text: If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be doing work I love.
phrases.use: Linking a past choice to your life now.

phrases.text: Every move is a bit of a gamble.
phrases.use: Admitting that any choice carries some risk.

items.meaning: A situation where you must choose between two options, and neither choice is easy or perfect.
items.example: Staying or leaving: it was a real dilemma.

items.meaning: The good points and the bad points of something you are deciding about.
items.example: We wrote down the pros and cons of each flat.

items.meaning: To think carefully about the good and bad sides of something before you decide.
items.example: Take a few days to weigh up the offer.

items.meaning: Doubts about a decision, just before or after you make it.
items.example: I had second thoughts the night before I signed the contract.

items.meaning: A strong sense that something is right or wrong, which you cannot fully explain.
items.example: My gut feeling was that the deal was too good to be true.

items.meaning: A natural way of knowing or reacting, without stopping to think it through.
items.example: Trust your instinct: if the job feels wrong, it probably is.

items.meaning: Suddenly, without planning or thinking about the results.
items.example: He bought the car on impulse and regretted it a week later.

items.meaning: To finally do something risky or important after thinking about it for a long time.
items.example: After years of renting, we took the plunge and bought a flat.

items.meaning: A risky action that could bring a good result or a bad one.
items.example: Leaving a permanent job for a small start-up was a gamble.

items.meaning: Careful to avoid risks or problems.
items.example: The bank was cautious about lending us more money.

items.meaning: To decide or promise firmly to do something, so it is hard to change your mind later.
items.example: Don't commit to a two-year contract until you've seen the office.

items.meaning: To accept something that is less than you really wanted.
items.example: They wanted a garden, but they settled for a balcony.

items.meaning: Steady, safe and not likely to change suddenly.
items.example: She gave up a stable job in a bank to retrain as a nurse.

items.meaning: A power that some people believe decides what happens in our lives.
items.example: Was it fate that we met on that train, or just luck?

items.meaning: Understanding a situation only after it has happened.
items.example: With hindsight, we should have waited another year.

sound.title: would've, not would of
sound.explain: In fast speech, have and had become short and weak. Would have sounds like would've, and if I had sounds like if I'd. Many people write would of, because that is what they hear, but the written form is always would have. Listen, then say each group.
lines: If I'd known, I would've waited.
I might've stayed another year.
I needn't have sold my car.

sayIt.instructions: Say Priya's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Are have and had short and light, with the stress on the main verbs?
lines: If I'd known how lonely the first winter would be, I might have waited a year.
I wish I'd asked more questions about the team before I committed to the move.
Yes. If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be doing work I love.
Maybe. Talk to the team in Glasgow first. I wish somebody had told me that.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. None of them describes what simply happened. Each one looks back at the past in a different way.
examples: If I'd known how lonely the first winter would be, I might have waited a year.
If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be doing work I love.
I wish I'd asked more questions about the team.
I needn't have sold my car.
spot.question: Which two sentences imagine a different past? Which of those two ends in the present? Which sentence is a regret? And which one describes something Priya did that was not necessary?
spot.answer: The first two imagine a different past. The first stays in the past: had known, might have waited. The second is mixed: a past if half (hadn't moved) and a result now (wouldn't be doing). I wish I'd asked is a regret: wish + had + past participle. I needn't have sold my car means she did sell it, and it turned out to be unnecessary.

rules.title: Third and mixed conditionals
rule: Third: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.
If I had known, I would have waited. (I didn't know, so I didn't wait.)
Less sure? Use might have or could have: I might have stayed.
Mixed: a past if half, a result now: If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be here now.
In speech: If I'd known, I'd have waited.
rules.mistake: Not: If I would have known, I would have waited. Say: If I had known, I would have waited.

rules.title: Regrets, and things you did not need to do
rule: wish or if only + had + past participle: I wish I had asked. If only I'd listened.
If only is stronger, and often more emotional.
I needn't have sold my car = I sold it, and it was not necessary.
I didn't need to sell my car = it was not necessary, and usually I didn't sell it.
rules.mistake: Not: I wish I would have asked. Say: I wish I had asked.

practice.q: If I ___ about the traffic, I would have left earlier.
practice.why: The if half of a third conditional takes had + past participle.

practice.q: If we had booked earlier, we ___ so much for the flights.
practice.why: The result half of a third conditional: would have + past participle.

practice.q: If I hadn't learnt English, I ___ this job now.
practice.why: A mixed conditional: a past if half, and a result now.

practice.q: I'm so tired. I wish I ___ to bed earlier last night.
practice.why: A regret about the past: wish + had + past participle.

practice.q: ___ I had checked the date! The office was closed when I got there.
practice.why: If only + had + past participle is a strong regret.

practice.q: We ___ have booked a table. The restaurant was almost empty.
practice.why: We booked, and it was not necessary: we needn't have booked.

practice.q: The meeting was cancelled, so I ___ go into the office. I worked from home instead.
practice.why: It was not necessary, and I did not go: didn't need to.

practice.q: If I had ___ about the vacancy, I would have applied.
I wish you ___ me. I would have helped.
practice.why: A regret about the past: wish + had + past participle.

practice.q: With ___, I can see it was the right decision.
practice.why: Hindsight is understanding something after it has happened.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a decision you made in the last few years: a job, a move, a course, something you bought. Write three sentences about it: one third conditional, one mixed conditional, and one sentence with wish or if only.
starters: If I had …, I would have …
If I hadn't …, I wouldn't be …
yourTurn.model: Two years ago, I bought a second-hand van to start a delivery business. If I had checked it more carefully, I would have noticed the rust. But if I hadn't bought it, I wouldn't have my own business now. I wish I had asked a mechanic to look at it first.

text.title: The job I nearly didn't take
text.body:
LOOKING BACK · a weekly column by Amina Okafor
PRACTICE TEXT: the writer and the magazine are invented.

Five years ago, I was offered a job running a small bakery café in Bristol, three hundred miles from everything I knew. I had a stable job in insurance, a flat I loved and friends I saw every week. I said no. Then, two days later, I rang back and said yes.

Readers often write to this column about decisions like mine, so this week I want to reflect on how mine turned out.

The sacrifices were real. I took a big cut in pay, and the financial security I had built up over ten years disappeared almost overnight. Relocating at thirty-eight is harder than at twenty-two: nobody invites you to the pub on your first Friday. The first year brought one setback after another. The oven broke in my second week, and a new coffee chain opened across the road.

If I'm honest, I nearly gave up that winter. If my sister hadn't driven down to help me paint the walls, I might have gone home.

The outcome? The café now employs six people, and the work is more fulfilling than anything I did in insurance. But I have had to come to terms with what I lost. I missed my best friend's wedding because I couldn't close for the day. I wish I had found a way to be there.

People ask me whether it was worth the uncertainty. With hindsight, yes, but I don't think the lesson is 'always take the risk'. If I had stayed, I would have had a good life too, just a different one. The lesson is smaller than that: weigh it up properly, and then, once you have committed, stop asking what would have happened. I needn't have spent those first months looking back. The only road you can see is the one you are on.

gist.q: What is the column mainly about?
gist.a: a decision the writer made five years ago, and how she sees it now
wrong: how to open a café in Bristol
why readers should always take risks
gist.why: She looks back on her move and reflects on what came of it.

gist.q: How does the writer feel about her decision now?
gist.a: glad she made it, but honest about what it cost her
wrong: sure that it was a mistake
gist.why: She says it was worth it, but she has had to come to terms with what she lost.

detail.q: What did the writer do when she was first offered the job?
detail.a: She said no, then changed her mind two days later.
wrong: She asked for more money first.
detail.why: She said no. Then, two days later, she rang back and said yes.

detail.q: Which of these was a setback in her first year?
detail.a: The oven broke in her second week.
wrong: She lost her flat in Bristol.
The café had to close for a month.
detail.why: The column says: The oven broke in my second week.

detail.q: What does she say might have happened if her sister hadn't helped?
wrong: She would have painted the walls herself.
She would have sold the café.
detail.why: If my sister hadn't driven down to help me, I might have gone home.
She says: I wish I had found a way to be there.

items.meaning: A regular article in a newspaper or magazine by the same writer, often about their own views or life.
items.example: She writes a weekly column about money.

items.meaning: To think carefully and seriously about something, especially something in the past.
items.example: It's worth taking an hour to reflect on what went wrong.

items.meaning: The final result of a decision, a process or an event.
items.example: Nobody could predict the outcome of the interview.

items.meaning: Something valuable that you give up to get something more important.
items.example: Moving abroad was a big sacrifice: I left my whole family behind.

items.meaning: To move to a new place to live or work, often because of a job.
items.example: The company is relocating its head office to Manchester.

items.meaning: A situation in which you do not know what will happen.
items.example: The uncertainty of waiting for the results was the hardest part.

items.meaning: Connected with money.
items.example: We had some financial problems after the business closed.

items.meaning: The feeling of being safe, without worrying about money, your job or the future.
items.example: A permanent contract gives you some security.

items.meaning: Making you feel satisfied, because what you do is useful or meaningful.
items.example: Teaching adults is hard work, but it is very fulfilling.

items.meaning: A problem that stops progress or makes a situation worse for a time.
items.example: Losing our biggest customer was a serious setback.

items.meaning: To slowly accept a sad or difficult situation.
items.example: It took him a year to come to terms with losing his job.

model.title: A reflective paragraph
model.body: Three years ago, I turned down a place on a nursing course because I was worried about money. At the time, it felt like the cautious, sensible choice: I had a stable job in a shop, and I needed the financial security. Looking back, I think I weighed up the pros and cons too quickly. If I had asked about grants, I would have found out that the course was almost free for adults like me. If I had taken that place, I would be a qualified nurse now. I wish I had asked more questions. However, I have come to terms with it, and I have learned something useful: when a decision feels too big, I get more information before I say no. Next year, I am applying again.

write.task: Write a reflective paragraph of 100–150 words about a decision you made. Say what you decided and why, what it cost you or gave you, and how you see it now. Use at least one third or mixed conditional and one sentence with wish or if only.
write.starter: A few years ago, I decided to …
checklist: I said what I decided, and why.
I used a third or mixed conditional: If I had …, I would have …
I used wish or if only + had: I wish I had …
I ended with what I learned, or how I see the decision now.

card.title: Talk through a real decision
card.situation: Choose a real decision from your own life: a job, a move, a course, a big purchase, or a time you said no to something. It does not have to be dramatic. Other people will ask you about it.
card.goal: Explain what you decided and why, what might have happened if you had chosen differently, and what you learned. Then answer questions.

phrases: A few years ago, I had to decide whether to … or …
I weighed up the pros and cons, but in the end I went with my gut feeling.
If I had …, I would probably have …
If I hadn't …, I wouldn't be … now.
I wish I had … / I needn't have …
With hindsight, what I learned is that …
prepare.notes: Write short notes, not full sentences: the decision, your reasons, the other option, one thing you regret or did not need to do, and what you learned. Think of one question someone might ask you, and your answer.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, each learner talks for about two minutes about their decision. The others listen and ask at least one question each: What would you have done if …? Do you ever have second thoughts? Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You are a friendly colleague having coffee with me. I will tell you about a big decision I made in the past. Listen, then ask me questions about it: why I decided, what might have happened if I had chosen differently, and what I learned. Ask one question at a time. After five questions, tell me which conditional sentences I used well, and correct any mistakes with wish or would have.

model.title: The flat we didn't buy
lines: Kwame
A few years ago, my wife and I had to decide whether to buy a flat in the city centre or keep renting.
Lena
That's a big one. What did you decide?
Kwame
We weighed up the pros and cons for months. The flat was perfect, but the price was high, so in the end we were cautious and kept renting.
Lena
Do you ever have second thoughts?
Kwame
Sometimes. If we had bought it, we would have paid a lot less than it costs now. Prices went up by almost a third.
Lena
So do you regret it?
Kwame
Partly. I wish we had looked at the figures more carefully. But if we'd bought it, we wouldn't have been able to take the job offer in Leeds a year later.
Lena
Oh, so it worked out in the end.
Kwame
In a way, yes. And we needn't have worried so much about money. My new job pays better.
Lena
What did you learn from it?
Kwame
With hindsight, I learned that there is no perfect decision. You choose, you commit, and you stop asking what would have happened.
compare: Did you say clearly what you decided and why?
Did you use a third or mixed conditional: If we had …, we would have …?
Did you use wish + had, or needn't have, correctly?
Did you finish with what you learned?

canDo: I can say what would have happened if a past decision had been different.
I can link a past choice to my life now with a mixed conditional.
I can talk about regrets with wish and if only.
I can write a reflective paragraph about a decision.
I can talk through a real decision and answer questions about it.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first paragraph. What decision does the main person face? What do you think they will choose?
reading.talk: At which moment could things have gone differently? What would you have done in the same situation? Write three or four sentences with If I had been …, I would have …, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.q: If I ___ the email, I would have replied.
quiz.why: The if half of a third conditional: had + past participle.

quiz.q: If she hadn't moved to Leeds, she ___ her husband.
quiz.why: The result half of a third conditional: would have + past participle.

quiz.q: If I had studied harder at school, I ___ a better job now.
quiz.why: A mixed conditional: a past if half, and a result now.

quiz.q: I wish I ___ to my manager before I resigned.
quiz.why: A regret about the past: wish + had + past participle.

quiz.q: We took a taxi, but the station was only five minutes away. We ___ have taken a taxi.
quiz.why: They took one, and it was not necessary: needn't have.

quiz.q: After months of thinking about it, she finally ___ and opened her own shop.
quiz.why: To take the plunge is to finally do something risky.

quiz.q: Leaving a permanent job to travel for a year was a ___ , but it paid off.
quiz.why: A gamble is a risky action that could go well or badly.

quiz.q: Someone you have just met says: I work in logistics. You want to keep the conversation going. What do you say?
options: Oh, do you? What does that involve?
Right. Well, nice to meet you.
quiz.a: Oh, do you? What does that involve?
quiz.why: An echo question plus a follow-up question keeps a conversation going politely.

quiz.q: The instructions were not clear, so I ___ the form and had to fill it in again.
quiz.why: The prefix mis- means wrongly: misunderstood means understood wrongly.

quiz.q: By the time the bus came, we ___ for forty minutes.
quiz.why: had been + -ing: something that continued up to a point in the past.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Priya and Tomasz's conversation in pairs, then a regret chain: each learner says one small decision (I took the bus), and the next says what would have happened if they hadn't.
Day 2: the task. Each learner talks through a real decision for two minutes; the others ask at least one question each. Note good conditionals and wish sentences for feedback at the end.
Day 3: talk about the book: where could the story have gone differently? Then two or three learners read their reflective paragraphs aloud, and the group suggests one improvement for each.
